Vignette:
# Priya Sharma

Priya Sharma was twenty-eight when the building collapsed. She had been a junior policy analyst at the City Planning Department then, newly promoted and eager to prove herself on a mixed-use development project in the warehouse district. The structure was a century-old manufacturing plant being retrofitted into apartments and retail space. On a Tuesday morning in March, she was inside conducting a final inspection before the city signed off on the conversion. She was standing in the central atrium, reviewing structural diagrams with the project manager, when she heard a sound like the world cracking—a deep, spreading groan of metal and concrete giving way. The collapse took seconds. The ceiling above the eastern wing fell first, and then the failure cascaded. She ran toward the exit, her legs moving faster than her mind could process what was happening, and made it through the main doors as the structure behind her folded in on itself. Dust filled the street. She stood on the sidewalk, coughing, her hands shaking, watching emergency vehicles arrive. Three workers died in the rubble. The project manager, who had been standing two feet from her, was never found intact.

In the weeks after, Priya returned to work. She had to. The city launched an investigation; there were depositions, reviews of the engineering reports she had signed off on, questions about whether she had missed something, whether her inexperience had contributed to the deaths. She hadn't missed anything—the original structural assessment had been falsified by the contractor—but the doubt had already taken root. She came to believe that the world operated on hidden dangers, that catastrophe was always present, waiting for the moment you let your guard down. If she had been standing two feet to the left, she would have died. The randomness of it terrified her.

Four years later, Priya is a City Council Member, elected on a platform of infrastructure safety and accountability. Her colleagues describe her as meticulous, thorough, relentless in her questioning of contractors and engineers. What they don't see is the machinery running underneath. Every morning before dawn, Priya lies awake, her mind cycling through the day ahead—the meetings, the people, the spaces she will move through. She has come to believe that she must be on guard all the time, that constant vigilance is the only thing standing between herself and another catastrophe. At night, the city feels different to her. The darkness makes her uncertain about what is happening around her, and she finds it harder to feel safe. She keeps her bedroom door open so she can hear if something is wrong. She sleeps poorly.

When she enters a building for a council meeting or a site visit, she identifies the exits before she sits down. She knows the stairs, the side doors, the windows that open onto fire escapes. In unfamiliar places—a new restaurant, a conference venue, a colleague's home—she avoids going altogether. She cannot assess the danger in spaces she hasn't mapped, and the anxiety of not knowing is worse than the disappointment of declining the invitation. Her social life has narrowed. She hasn't been on a date in three years. The thought of being in someone else's apartment, in a space she doesn't control, where she can't identify escape routes, is unbearable.

She also avoids physical stress. She stopped running six months ago; the elevated heart rate felt too close to panic, and she couldn't distinguish between her body's normal response to exertion and the beginning of a threat response. She stopped going to the gym. She takes the elevator instead of the stairs. She is hypervigilant toward people—watching faces, postures, the way someone holds their hands—trying to spot danger before it manifests. She scans every environment she enters, a habit so automatic now that she barely notices she is doing it.

Three weeks ago, during a particularly tense budget meeting, a contractor raised his voice in disagreement with her. He wasn't angry at her specifically; he was frustrated with the process. But Priya felt her body flood with fear. Her hands trembled. She excused herself and went to her office, where she sat in the dark for an hour, certain that something terrible was about to happen. That night, she couldn't sleep. The next morning, she called a therapist. She is afraid that this vigilance, this constant bracing for disaster, is the only thing keeping her alive—and she is exhausted. She wants to feel safe again, but she is terrified of what might happen if she stops watching.
